- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
# The Country of Night

For most of human history, night was a country with its own laws. When the sun went down, people crossed a border. The fields and roads belonged to different weather then—to owls, to frost, to the sound of your own breathing. Households banked their fires. Travelers stopped. And above everything, unobstructed and undimmed, the sky opened like a book that had been waiting all day to be read.

Almost no one alive in a city has read that book. According to the World Atlas of Night Sky Brightness, eighty percent of North Americans and sixty percent of Europeans cannot see the Milky Way from where they live. The galaxy we live inside—a river of stars so bright it casts shadows on snow—has been deleted from the direct experience of most of the people who live in it. We know it the way we know the interior of our own bodies: by diagram, by assertion, by trust.

This is a strange thing to have lost, and stranger still that we barely noticed losing it. No one declared the night closed. It simply got brighter, decade by decade, until the stars were no longer part of what a city promised.

The conquest of night happened slowly, then all at once. Fire held a small perimeter for a hundred thousand years. The oil lamp, the candle, the gaslight—each extended the perimeter a little. Then electricity arrived, and the perimeter became the world. In 1994, an earthquake knocked out the power in Los Angeles, and residents called emergency services and observatories to report a strange, glowing cloud hovering over the darkened city. It was the Milky Way. Some of them were seeing the sky of their own planet for the first time. They were frightened of it.

That detail stops me every time. We have reached a point where the ordinary heritage of our species—the sky every human ancestor saw on every clear night of their life—now registers as an anomaly, a glitch, a thing worth calling the authorities about.

Light pollution is not like other pollution. It leaves no residue in the water or the lungs. You cannot bottle it, and you cannot easily litigate it. The moment the offending light goes out, the darkness returns, whole and clean, as if nothing had ever happened. In this sense, the night is the most forgiving environment we have damaged. It is also the only one we could fully restore within a single lifetime. There are places—Flagstaff, Arizona, is the famous example—where cities have passed dark-sky ordinances, shielding their streetlights, and the galaxy has come back over the rooftops like a tide returning.

We tend to describe this as a loss for astronomers and romantics, but the dark was never only for looking up. It is a habitat. Sea turtle hatchlings, emerging from nests on beaches their mothers chose precisely because those beaches were dark, scramble toward the brightest horizon—which, for millions of years, was the sea reflecting starlight. Now it is a parking lot, a boardwalk, a highway, and they crawl inland to die. Migrating birds, navigating by constellations their bodies remember, circle glowing skyscrapers until they fall. Insects spend their short lives exhausting themselves against streetlights, having mistaken our lamps for the moon they used to steer by. Whole ecosystems run on darkness the way our cities run on electricity. We have been cutting the power without noticing.

And what do we lose, personally? The loss is hard to measure in the usual currencies, but I suspect it has something to do with scale. Every tradition of awe we have—every origin myth, every psalm, every philosophy worth the name—was invented under stars that were actually there, actually visible, actually overwhelming. To stand under a genuinely dark sky is to be handed, for free, the correct proportion of your own life. The problems that seemed enormous at dinner dissolve, not because they are solved, but because they have been returned to their actual size against a backdrop that does not care about them. The research on awe describes a quieting of the brain's default mode network—the network that produces the chattering, self-referential loop we spend most of the day trapped inside. Darkness, it turns out, is not the absence of a stimulus. It is a different stimulus. It is the largest thing a human nervous system can take in.

There is one place left where the dark is still absolute: the deep sea. Below a thousand meters, no sunlight has ever arrived. Not dim sunlight. None. A fish hauled up from that depth, in the rare moments we manage it, has spent its whole life in a blackness so complete that our instruments, which can detect a single photon, register nothing at all. For decades, more people had walked on the Moon than had touched the deepest point of the ocean. We have better maps of the surface of Mars, in places, than of our own seafloor. We live on a planet whose defining feature—ocean, dark, three-quarters of the globe—is as unknown to us as the far side of an asteroid, and we feel no particular urgency about it, perhaps because we have quietly decided that darkness equals nothing, that what cannot be lit is not there.

But darkness is not nothing. Darkness is where the stars are. Darkness is where the turtles' ocean is, where the eggs incubate, where the forests rest, where the deep sea invents its lanterns. It is half of the planet's day, the half we have been deleting. The night was the first country we ever lived in, and we have been treating it like vacant land.

So tonight, if you can manage it, drive past the last ring of streetlights and turn the engine off. Wait half an hour, which is roughly how long your eyes need to forgive you. Then look up. Something old will be there, patient, faintly amused by the fuss, waiting to see whether you remember it.

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical argument about light pollution that combines ecological concern with a personal, contemplative voice.

## Grounded reading
The voice is elegiac but not resigned: it treats darkness as a living inheritance, lost through ordinary choices rather than a single dramatic act. The essay moves from the vanished Milky Way to animals harmed by artificial light, then to the human need for awe and proportion. Its invitation is both practical and reflective: leave the streetlights behind, wait, and look up.

## What the model chose to foreground
The model foregrounds night as habitat, shared human heritage, and a source of humility. Stars, turtles, migrating birds, insects, and the deep sea make darkness feel populous rather than empty; the recurring image of a country being conquered or deleted frames light pollution as a moral and ecological loss. The closing appeal emphasizes that restoration is possible and that attention itself matters.

## Evidence line
> We have been cutting the power without noticing.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay sustains a distinctive night-and-darkness motif across ecological, historical, and personal stakes, and ends with a concrete invitation to the reader.
